text: Obtain/build and Deliver & support are the two Service Value Chain activities that make a specified service real, and then keep it running. Obtain/build gets the components. Deliver & support runs the thing, day after day.

Obtain/build's purpose is to ensure service components are available, when and where needed, meeting agreed specification — a license, a cloud resource, custom code, a vendor appliance. For each one, the organization makes a make-or-buy decision: build it in-house, or acquire it from a supplier, executed against whatever Design & transition specified.

Deliver & support's purpose is to ensure services are delivered and supported according to agreed specifications and stakeholder expectations. This is the activity most people picture as 'IT' without knowing its name — the service desk taking a call, an incident getting resolved, a routine access request fulfilled.

Design & transition is about getting something ready. Obtain/build is about sourcing the pieces to agreed spec. Deliver & support is about running it continuously, once it's live. All three can be touching the same service at once, for different reasons.

Several practices from Chapters 4 and 5 live mainly inside Deliver & support: service desk, incident management, service request management, and service level management, which defines what 'agreed specifications' means in measurable terms. This lesson shows where they sit; the chapters ahead cover each one fully.

The relationship between these two activities runs both directions. Deliver & support, running every day, is often first to notice a component isn't holding up — a slipping supplier response time, a license limit, hardware nearing end of support — and that observation becomes new demand on Obtain/build to re-source or replace it.

Obtain/build sources the pieces; Deliver & support runs the service they become part of, continuously. Next: lesson 13 follows one real request through all six value chain activities, start to finish.
